title: Mitzi
tagline: Glasses with a language tutor inside: they label your world, build your flashcards, and give you a friend to talk to who sees what you see.
status_text: Planning: idea, research and Phase 0 done; phone prototype next
tags: AR glasses, Language learning, Japanese, Computer vision, Voice AI, Spaced repetition (FSRS), 3D printing

timeline.title: Second session with Suki: yesterday's words came back
timeline.summary: The new tutor prompt worked: review first, then a short list of new words. All four review words came back after one day, three of them with help or a small slip. The next problem showed up too: Suki reads a transcript, so she can't judge sounds that differ only in length. She now says those words slowly and moves on.

timeline.title: First session with Suki, and a speaking-only path
timeline.summary: Ten minutes as a total beginner, in full sentences from the first object. It was too much too fast: 13 new items, and the longest sentence didn't stick. The tutor prompt now reviews first and adds at most 5 new items. One decision came out of it: these are glasses for speaking, so written Japanese is optional, and a Read mode for signs and menus comes later.

timeline.title: Why I'm building glasses that teach me Japanese
timeline.summary: My wife's grandmother speaks Japanese, and her English is limited. I'm learning Japanese from zero so I can talk with her in her own language, and I'm building the glasses that teach me. The project is named after her.

timeline.title: The plan: prove the learning before building the hardware
timeline.summary: Research shows labels on real objects beat flashcards. Mitzi adds labels that fade as you learn, a deck that builds itself from your own home, and Suki, a conversation partner who uses the words you're due to review. Step one is a phone prototype; the glasses come after the method works.
